chapter: Starting out in New York and Chicago
title: Seven-piece band, Bryce Roperson, and trumpeter Gail Brockman
summary: His Minneapolis-based seven-piece band, with white guitarist Bryce Roperson and trumpeter Gail Brockman who played the Red Top solo with Gene Ammons, joined Billy Williams' revue and went to Las Vegas.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: enough. I used to go down and stand down and watch these things. They said, you want to see guys go upstairs and come out with -- guys used to stand on the street sometime with a trumpet, saxophone, and fiddle. Violin, you know. (Inaudible) Waitin' for -- all gigs in New York. (unintelligible). Then you go to the Metropole, and you know the story of the Metropole. But getting back to a mixed group. We had quite a few fellas that would frequent Minton's, and I used to use a lot of mixed guys, a lot of them -- I don't remember their names. I've got 'em written down. I always kept a diary, things like that. I know I've got 'em around somewhere. But I had a great guitarist, believe it or not, right here in Denver that was in my group. He's a white boy. I don't know if you ever heard of him or not. He couldn't read a note as big as this room, but he could play it. He could play some of the greatest chords on the guitar. His name was Bryce Roperson. He was a student actually of the late and great T-Bone Walker. T-Bone taught him quite a few things. But this guy could play, and he was in my seven piece band that I had in later years that was booked into Minneapolis, Minnesota, and this guy joined me there. I think Minneapolis, Minnesota is the hometown of one of my greatest small bands. I had a 7-piece band. (Inaudible) Later, we joined the great Billy Williams in his revue review and went to Las Vegas with this band. I've got a picture of this group here. They weren't any individual names, but we played together, but the guys could play. The only guy that

I would mention that was in that seven piece group -- we're talking in the forties now -- was a trumpet player who was with me for 18 years, even in my Chicago band, and he just died recently -- Gayle Brockman was his name. I'll tell you. I know you'll know him. He's the guy that played the original trumpet solo with Jug. Jug is Gene Ammonds.

(Singing) This is Gayle Brockman. He could read specks, man. He's another one of these sight readers that you're playing in the first and second bar and his eyes are on the fourth and who had the Billy Williams Revue, fifth. In fact, Billie Williams, (unintelligible) thought he was God because he was playing trumpet on all the arrangements that I made for the review, and he was hitting those notes, and, oh man, he never let us down. He could always play when everybody else was tired. And he was a shy guy. He always kept his head down. It's the only trouble -- we could never get him to hold his head up, even on stage. He was shy. You look at him and he would -- he played with his eyes shut all the time. But man, he could play. There's another guy didn't know anything about chords, but he never ran a bad chord to a tune. He knew the changes. His ear was uncanny. If you asked him to run an F seventh, a D flat natural, or anything,
he'd look at you like you're crazy. But all you gotta do is hit it, and I'll bet you he would run it. That was -- these are great guys. That was my greatest band. Small band, I mean --
Yes, this is -- I see from this picture there's six here. And you had that what 15 years you say, or --
Yes. It was a long time.
